title: Graduate Accountant Salary: Converting Hourly Rates to Annual Pay in Australia
description: Learn how to convert a graduate accountant salary from hourly to annual using the 38-hour week, plus tax, super, and award rates from Fair Work and ABS data.
salarySummary: A typical graduate accountant salary of $55,000–$65,000 per year equates to roughly $28–$33 per hour based on a 38-hour week, before tax and super.

faqs.q: How is annual salary calculated from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52. For a standard full-time role, we assume 38 hours per week. For example, $30 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $59,280 per year. The fortnightly equivalent is your weekly pay multiplied by 2.

faqs.q: What is the national minimum wage in 2026?
faqs.a: From 1 July 2026, the national minimum wage is $26.44 per hour or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, making it $33.05 per hour. These rates are set by the Fair Work Commission and apply to award/agreement-free employees.

faqs.q: How does superannuation affect a graduate accountant salary?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your salary at 12% of ordinary earnings (for 2026–27), up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. If your annual salary is $60,000, your employer contributes an extra $7,200 into your super fund. This is not included in your take-home pay.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Graduate Accountant Salary in Australia

If you’re starting your career as an accountant, one of the first questions you’ll ask is: what is a typical **graduate accountant salary**? Whether you’ve been offered an hourly rate or an annual package, knowing how to convert between the two helps you compare offers and understand your take-home pay. This article explains the conversion using the standard 38-hour week, the national minimum wage, award rates, casual loading, tax, and superannuation.

## The Basic Conversion: Hourly to Annual

The standard formula for converting an hourly rate to an annual salary is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

We assume a full-time week of 38 ordinary hours, as defined by the Fair Work Commission. For example, if your hourly rate is $30:

- Weekly pay = $30 × 38 = $1,140
- Fortnightly pay = $1,140 × 2 = $2,280
- Annual gross = $1,140 × 52 = $59,280

This calculation assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. It’s a starting point for estimating your income.

## Graduate Accountant Salary: What the Data Shows

According to Jobs and Skills Australia, the median full-time earnings for all accountants (including experienced professionals) is $2,003 per week, or about $53 per hour. However, a **graduate accountant salary** typically starts lower. Entry-level roles often fall between $55,000 and $65,000 per year, which translates to roughly $28 to $33 per hour for a 38-hour week. This range sits above the national minimum wage but below the occupation’s median.

The Fair Work Ombudsman’s [pay guides](/blog) provide minimum rates for accountants covered by awards, such as the Professional Employees Award. Graduate accountants may be classified at a lower level, so checking the relevant award is important. If no award applies, the [national minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) of $26.44 per hour (from 1 July 2026) is the legal floor.

## Casual Loading and Award Rates

If you work as a casual employee, you are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base rate. For the national minimum wage, this gives $33.05 per hour. The same loading applies to award rates unless the award specifies a different casual loading. Our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains how to calculate it.

Award rates for accountants vary by classification and experience. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes updated pay guides each year. From 1 July 2026, award minimum wages increased by 4.75%. Always use the current pay guide for your award to find the correct minimum.

## Tax on Your Salary

Once you have your annual gross figure, you can estimate your take-home pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- Nil tax on income up to $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus, the Medicare levy of 2% applies to most taxpayers. For a graduate accountant earning $60,000, the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be roughly $8,667, leaving a take-home pay of about $51,333 per year. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool for a more detailed estimate.

## Superannuation: Paid on Top

Superannuation is an additional contribution your employer must make. For 2026–27, the super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. This is paid on top of your salary, not deducted from it. For a $60,000 salary, your employer adds $7,200 to your super fund annually. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for more.

## Comparing Offers: Hourly vs Salary

When comparing a **graduate accountant salary** offer, consider whether it’s expressed as an hourly rate or an annual package. Use the formula above to convert both to the same basis. Remember that salaried roles may include paid leave and other entitlements, while hourly roles may offer overtime or penalty rates. The [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) guide can help.

## Other Pay Points to Know

The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that full-time adult ordinary-time earnings average $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). This is higher than the typical graduate accountant salary, reflecting the mix of experienced workers. For a broader view of earnings across occupations, visit our [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page.

## Final Thoughts

Understanding how to convert your hourly rate to an annual salary is essential for negotiating and budgeting. Whether you’re starting as a graduate accountant or considering a casual role, the 38-hour week, award rates, tax, and super all affect your final pay. Use the [job pay](/topics/job-pay) resources to compare roles and ensure you’re being paid correctly.

*Disclaimer: Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.*
